entries.meaning: The flat upper surface of a table. ---
examples: The tabletop is solid walnut.
Wipe the tabletop before you set the plates down.
Years of homework had scratched the tabletop.

entries.meaning: A short nail with a broad flat head, used to fasten something to a surface. ---
examples: She hung the poster with four tacks.
A tack was stuck in the front tire.
Push the map into the corkboard with a tack.

entries.meaning: The skill of saying and doing things without upsetting people. ---
examples: He handled the complaint with real tact.
It takes tact to tell someone their work is not good enough.
She has no tact whatsoever.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse tact (politeness) with tack (a small nail, or a course of action).

entries.meaning: A particular action chosen to reach a short-term goal. ---
examples: Delaying the vote was a smart tactic.
Their tactics have not changed in years.
The company uses pressure tactics on customers who pay late.

entries.meaning: A chewy candy made by boiling sugar and pulling it until it is soft and glossy. ---
examples: We bought saltwater taffy on the boardwalk.
The kids pulled taffy at the fall festival.
A piece of taffy stuck to his back teeth.

entries.meaning: A thick paste made from ground sesame seeds. ---
examples: Hummus is chickpeas, lemon, garlic, and tahini.
Stir the tahini well before you measure it out.
The dressing is just tahini thinned with water.

entries.meaning: A steep out-of-control fall, either of an airplane or of something like prices or a mood. ---
examples: The news sent the stock into a tailspin.
The plane went into a tailspin over the desert.
After the layoff he went into an emotional tailspin.

entries.meaning: A wind blowing from behind, which helps you move faster. ---
examples: A strong tailwind got us to Denver twenty minutes early.
Cyclists love a tailwind on the ride home.
Low interest rates were a tailwind for the housing market.

entries.meaning: Someone's particular opinion on a subject, or one filmed attempt at a scene. ---
examples: What is your take on the new policy?
The director kept the third take.
Her take on the book is worth reading.

entries.meaning: The main point you are meant to remember from a talk, meeting, or article. ---
examples: The big takeaway is that costs are rising faster than sales.
Here are three takeaways from last night's debate.
My takeaway from the class was to start earlier.
entries.contrast: In American English a takeaway is a main point; the British also use it for food ordered to go, which Americans call takeout.

entries.meaning: A very soft mineral ground into the fine white powder used on skin. ---
examples: The powder is mostly talc and cornstarch.
Some baby powders no longer contain talc.
Talc is the softest mineral on the hardness scale.
entries.contrast: The mineral is talc; the product sold for skin is usually called talcum powder.

entries.meaning: A speech or a serious conversation about a particular subject. ---
examples: She gave a talk on climate policy.
We need to have a talk about your grades.
There are three talks before lunch.

entries.meaning: A Mexican dish of seasoned corn dough steamed in a corn husk, usually around a filling. ---
examples: His grandmother makes tamales every Christmas.
I ordered a pork tamale and a side of rice.
The tamales come wrapped in husks that you peel off.
entries.contrast: One is a tamale, two are tamales; the husk is never eaten.

entries.meaning: A sour-sweet tropical fruit pod used in sauces, candy, and drinks. ---
examples: The sauce gets its tang from tamarind.
She bought a block of tamarind paste at the Asian market.
Tamarind soda is sold in every corner store there.

entries.meaning: A pair working together, or a bicycle built for two riders one behind the other. ---
examples: The two agencies worked in tandem on the rescue.
They rented a tandem at the beach.
The two drugs are given in tandem.

entries.meaning: A line that touches a curve at one point, or a sudden change of subject. ---
examples: He went off on a tangent about his car.
The lecture kept wandering onto tangents.
Draw a tangent to the circle at point A.

entries.meaning: A dramatic ballroom dance from Argentina, or the music written for it. ---
examples: They danced a slow tango at the reception.
The band played two tangos in a row.
She has been taking tango lessons since March.

entries.meaning: A bitter natural substance in tea, red wine, and tree bark that dries the mouth. ---
examples: This wine has firm tannins.
Tea left to steep too long tastes of tannin.
Tannins soften as the wine ages in the bottle.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A long flat worm that lives in the intestines of a person or animal. ---
examples: The vet found a tapeworm in the cat.
Undercooked pork can carry tapeworms.
One dose of the medicine kills the tapeworm.

entries.meaning: A starch from the cassava root, used in puddings and in the chewy pearls in bubble tea. ---
examples: She made tapioca pudding for dessert.
The drink is full of tapioca pearls.
Tapioca thickens the pie filling without clouding it.

entries.meaning: A large sheet of waterproof cloth or plastic used as a cover. ---
examples: They threw a tarpaulin over the woodpile.
The damaged roof was patched with a blue tarpaulin.
Two tarpaulins covered the infield during the rain delay.
entries.contrast: In everyday American speech this is almost always shortened to tarp.

entries.meaning: A narrow-leaved herb with a mild licorice flavor, common in French cooking. ---
examples: The sauce needs fresh tarragon.
Tarragon goes well with chicken and eggs.
She grows tarragon in a pot on the deck.

entries.meaning: An open pastry shell filled with fruit or cream and baked without a top crust. ---
examples: She brought a lemon tart to dinner.
The bakery sells small fruit tarts by the register.
This tart has a shortbread crust.

entries.meaning: A child who tells adults about other children's misbehavior. ---
examples: Nobody likes a tattletale.
His little sister is a total tattletale.
The other kids called him a tattletale for a week.

entries.meaning: A permanent design made by putting ink under the skin. ---
examples: He has a tattoo of an anchor on his forearm.
Both of her arms are covered in tattoos.
Getting a tattoo removed takes several sessions.

entries.meaning: A grayish-brown color often used in clothing and home decorating. ---
examples: The walls are painted a soft taupe.
She chose taupe for the new curtains.
Taupe goes with almost anything.
entries.contrast: Said TOHP, rhyming with hope — not TAWP and not two syllables.

entries.meaning: A system for sorting things into named groups, especially living things. ---
examples: Linnaeus created the taxonomy we still use for species.
The team built a taxonomy of customer complaints.
Different taxonomies place the fungus in different families.

entries.meaning: The work or profession of giving lessons. ---
examples: She went into teaching right after college.
Teaching pays less than she expected.
He splits his time between research and teaching.

entries.meaning: A hard, oily tropical wood used for outdoor furniture and boat decks. ---
examples: The patio set is solid teak.
Teak holds up well in rain and sun.
The whole deck was laid in teak.

entries.meaning: A covered pot with a spout and handle for boiling water on a stove. ---
examples: The teakettle started whistling.
Put the teakettle on, would you?
She keeps a copper teakettle on the back burner.
entries.contrast: A teakettle boils the water on the stove; the pot you brew the tea in is a teapot.

entries.meaning: A single drop of the liquid that comes from crying, or a shape like it. ---
examples: A teardrop rolled down her cheek.
The pendant is shaped like a teardrop.
He has a small teardrop tattooed under one eye.

entries.meaning: A movie, book, or song made to bring the audience to tears. ---
examples: Bring tissues, because it is a real tearjerker.
The channel shows holiday tearjerkers all December.
The last chapter is a tearjerker.

entries.meaning: A short advertisement or clip meant to stir up interest in something coming later. ---
examples: The studio released a thirty-second teaser.
The subject line is just a teaser to get you to open the email.
They posted two teasers before the full trailer.

entries.meaning: Someone who is skilled at or very interested in computers and technology. ---
examples: Ask a techie to set up the router.
The neighborhood is full of young techies.
He is the family techie.

entries.meaning: A small point of rules or law that can decide a case even though it seems unimportant. ---
examples: The case was thrown out on a technicality.
He won the argument on a technicality.
Let us not get lost in technicalities.

entries.meaning: A style of fast electronic dance music built on repeating machine-made beats. ---
examples: The club plays techno until four in the morning.
He has been into techno since high school.
Techno came out of Detroit in the 1980s.

entries.meaning: The study of how the huge plates of the earth's crust move and reshape the surface. ---
examples: Plate tectonics explains why earthquakes cluster along the coast.
The class spent a week on tectonics.
Tectonics raised the Himalayas over millions of years.
entries.contrast: Though it ends in -s, tectonics takes a singular verb: plate tectonics explains, not explain.

entries.meaning: Someone who never drinks alcohol. ---
examples: He has been a teetotaler since college.
The host keeps juice on hand for the teetotalers.
As a teetotaler, she always ends up driving everyone home.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l — teetotaler; British writing doubles it as teetotaller.

entries.meaning: A short message that used to be sent by telegraph and delivered on paper. ---
examples: Her family got the telegram two weeks after he died.
People sent telegrams before long-distance calls got cheap.
The telegram was only eight words long.

entries.meaning: A nineteenth-century system, or the machine used for it, that sent messages as signals over wires. ---
examples: News of the battle traveled by telegraph.
The museum has a working telegraph from 1870.
Early telegraphs could carry only one message at a time.

entries.meaning: Measurements taken at a distance and sent back automatically to a receiver. ---
examples: The spacecraft stopped sending telemetry an hour after launch.
Race engineers watch the car's telemetry from the pit wall.
You can turn off the app's telemetry in the privacy settings.

entries.meaning: A screen that shows a speaker's script so they can read it while facing the camera. ---
examples: The anchor read the whole story off a teleprompter.
Both teleprompters failed, so the senator spoke from memory.
He glanced at the teleprompter and lost his place.

entries.meaning: A protective cap at the end of a chromosome that gets shorter as cells divide. ---
examples: Telomeres grow shorter as we age.
The study measured telomere length in blood cells.
Each telomere shields the DNA underneath it.

entries.meaning: A worker hired for a short period, usually through an agency. ---
examples: They brought in a temp to cover the front desk.
Two temps handled the holiday rush.
She worked as a temp for a year before they hired her full time.
entries.contrast: In speech temp is also short for temperature, as in "check the temp on the oven."

entries.meaning: Moderation in drinking alcohol, or giving it up completely. ---
examples: The temperance movement helped bring about Prohibition.
She preached temperance at every church meeting.
The county's old temperance laws still ban Sunday sales.

entries.meaning: A violent storm, or a sudden burst of uproar. ---
examples: A tempest tore the roof off the boathouse.
One careless post set off a tempest in the comments.
Sailors have feared these tempests for centuries.

entries.meaning: A Japanese dish of seafood or vegetables fried in a light batter. ---
examples: We ordered shrimp tempura to start.
The tempura was crisp and not greasy at all.
She makes tempura with sparkling water in the batter.

entries.meaning: A habit of behaving in a certain way, or the general direction something moves in. ---
examples: He has a tendency to interrupt when he gets excited.
Prices show a tendency to rise in the spring.
Both kids have the same tendencies.

entries.meaning: A tool or powder used to make meat softer. ---
examples: Pound the steak with a tenderizer before you cook it.
She keeps a wooden tenderizer in the top drawer.
A little tenderizer helps with the tougher cuts.
entries.русский: молоток для отбивания мяса; размягчитель мяса
entries.contrast: British English spells it tenderiser, with an s.

entries.meaning: Gentle, caring feeling, or soreness in a part of the body when it is pressed. ---
examples: He spoke to his mother with real tenderness.
The doctor checked for tenderness around the knee.
There's still some tenderness where the bruise was.

entries.meaning: A cone-shaped tent of poles and hides used by Plains Indian peoples. ---
examples: The museum has a full-size tepee set up outside.
Three tepees stood at the edge of the camp.
The kids built a tepee out of branches and a tarp.
entries.contrast: Also spelled teepee and tipi; all three are said TEE-pee.

entries.meaning: A unit of computer storage equal to about a thousand gigabytes. ---
examples: The new drive holds two terabytes.
A single terabyte isn't much for video work.
We back up about a terabyte of data every night.

entries.meaning: A sweet Japanese sauce made with soy sauce, or food grilled in it. ---
examples: I ordered chicken teriyaki with brown rice.
She brushed teriyaki on the salmon before broiling it.
The teriyaki was a little too sweet for me.

entries.meaning: A small turtle that lives in fresh or slightly salty water. ---
examples: A terrapin was sunning itself on the log.
The bay is home to diamondback terrapins.
We found two baby terrapins by the pond.

entries.meaning: A pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps and no overlaps. ---
examples: The bathroom floor is a tessellation of hexagons.
Escher's prints are full of tessellations.
We drew a tessellation in geometry class.

entries.meaning: A person or device that tests something, or a sample of a product for customers to try. ---
examples: The studio hired two testers for the beta.
Use the tester on the counter before you buy the lipstick.
He works as a game tester on the night shift.

entries.meaning: The process of checking how something works or whether someone has a condition. ---
examples: Drug testing is required for every driver.
The software goes into testing next week.
Free testing was set up at the public library.

entries.meaning: The main male sex hormone. ---
examples: His doctor checked his testosterone levels.
Testosterone drops slowly as men get older.
The locker room was all noise and testosterone.

entries.meaning: A serious disease caused by bacteria entering a wound, which stiffens the muscles. ---
examples: She got a tetanus shot after stepping on a nail.
Tetanus is rare here because most children are vaccinated.
The clinic gives tetanus boosters every ten years.

entries.meaning: A playground game in which two players hit a ball on a rope around a pole. ---
examples: We played tetherball every recess in fourth grade.
The school put in a new tetherball pole.
He is still unbeatable at tetherball.

entries.meaning: A solid shape with four triangular faces. ---
examples: A tetrahedron has four faces and four corners.
She folded the paper into a small tetrahedron.
The model was built out of plastic tetrahedrons.
entries.contrast: Everyday plural is tetrahedrons; math writing often uses tetrahedra.

entries.meaning: A poetic meter with four beats in each line. ---
examples: The poem is written in iambic tetrameter.
Tetrameter moves faster than pentameter.
He switched to tetrameter halfway through the sequence.

entries.meaning: A structure deep in the brain that passes signals from the senses to the cortex. ---
examples: The thalamus relays almost everything the senses pick up.
Damage to the thalamus can disrupt sleep.
The scan showed swelling near the thalamus.
entries.contrast: The plural is thalami, said THAL-uh-my.

entries.meaning: Belief in a god, especially one who takes an active part in the world. ---
examples: The course compares theism and atheism.
His argument for theism rests on the idea of design.
She moved from theism to agnosticism during college.

entries.meaning: A government run by religious leaders or according to religious law. ---
examples: The revolution turned the country into a theocracy.
He warned that the new law was a step toward theocracy.
Few theocracies last long in the modern world.

entries.meaning: Someone who studies religion and religious belief. ---
examples: The theologian spoke at the divinity school last night.
Two theologians debated the passage for an hour.
She's a theologian who writes for a general audience.

entries.meaning: A mathematical statement that has been proved to be true. ---
examples: We proved the theorem in class today.
The Pythagorean theorem is the one everybody remembers.
His proof of the theorem runs two hundred pages.

entries.meaning: Someone who develops ideas that explain how something works. ---
examples: She's a leading theorist of urban planning.
The theorists disagree about what caused the collapse.
As a political theorist, he writes more than he teaches.

entries.meaning: The layer of the atmosphere above the mesosphere, where temperature rises with height. ---
examples: The space station orbits inside the thermosphere.
Auroras form high up in the thermosphere.
The thermosphere begins about fifty miles up.

entries.meaning: An object, event, or matter that you do not name more exactly. ---
examples: What's that thing on the top shelf?
A few things still bother me about the plan.
The best thing about the job is the people.

entries.meaning: A person who thinks deeply, especially one with important ideas. ---
examples: He was one of the great thinkers of his generation.
She's a careful thinker and a slow writer.
The book profiles six thinkers who changed economics.

entries.meaning: The activity of using your mind, or a person's current view on a question. ---
examples: The class is meant to teach critical thinking.
My thinking on this has changed a lot since March.
Wishful thinking won't balance the budget.

entries.meaning: Underwear or a sandal with a narrow strip that passes between the legs or toes, or a thin strip of leather. ---
examples: She wore a thong under the thin dress.
The sandal's thong snapped on the beach.
He tied the bundle shut with a leather thong.
entries.contrast: In Australia thongs are flip-flops; in the US the word usually means underwear.

entries.meaning: A horse of pure breeding, especially one bred for racing. ---
examples: Her grandfather raised thoroughbreds in Kentucky.
The thoroughbred won by two lengths.
He paid far too much for an untested thoroughbred.

entries.meaning: Careful attention to every detail of a job. ---
examples: The inspector's thoroughness impressed everyone.
I admire her thoroughness, even when it slows us down.
The report was praised for its thoroughness.

entries.meaning: Careful, economical use of money. ---
examples: Her thrift got the family through the recession.
He runs the shop with old-fashioned thrift.
Thrift stores do good business when money is tight.

entries.meaning: A book, movie, or play with an exciting, suspenseful plot. ---
examples: I read a legal thriller on the flight.
The movie is a slow-burn thriller with a great ending.
She writes thrillers set in small towns.

entries.meaning: The ceremonial chair of a king or queen, or royal power itself. ---
examples: The queen sat on a gold throne.
He came to the throne at nineteen.
Two brothers fought over the throne for a decade.
entries.contrast: Throne sounds exactly like thrown, the past participle of throw.

entries.meaning: An act of throwing something, or a light blanket for a couch or chair. ---
examples: His throw to first base sailed wide.
She keeps a wool throw over the armchair.
Each player gets three throws.

entries.meaning: A songbird with a spotted breast and a musical call. ---
examples: A thrush sang from the hedge at dawn.
Thrushes nest in the woods behind the house.
The wood thrush is common in the eastern states.

entries.meaning: The mark left by the pattern of lines on the tip of a thumb. ---
examples: There was a greasy thumbprint on the screen.
The phone unlocks with my thumbprint.
Police found two clear thumbprints on the glass.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: THUM-print.

entries.meaning: A short pin with a wide flat head, pushed in with the thumb to hold paper on a board. ---
examples: She pinned the map up with four thumbtacks.
A thumbtack fell out of the corkboard.
Don't leave thumbtacks lying on the floor.
entries.contrast: American thumbtack is British drawing pin; the b is silent.

entries.meaning: A gland in the upper chest where cells of the immune system mature. ---
examples: The thymus shrinks as a person gets older.
T cells finish developing in the thymus.
Surgeons removed part of his thymus.

entries.meaning: A small repeated movement or sound that a person cannot fully control. ---
examples: He has a tic that makes him blink hard.
Her verbal tics show up when she's nervous.
The medication reduced his tics within a month.
entries.contrast: Tic sounds just like tick, the insect or the sound of a clock.

entries.meaning: A running display of stock prices or headlines, or the short code that identifies a stock. ---
examples: The ticker at the bottom of the screen showed the closing prices.
Apple trades under the ticker AAPL.
News tickers scrolled all through the broadcast.

entries.meaning: The state of being tight — stiff, stretched, or short of room or money. ---
examples: He felt a tightness in his chest and called 911.
The tightness of the schedule left no room for error.
There's still some tightness in my hamstrings.

entries.meaning: A sloping position, or the act of leaning something to one side. ---
examples: The picture hangs at a slight tilt.
A small tilt of her head told me she disagreed.
Give the pan a tilt so the butter spreads.

entries.meaning: The particular quality of a sound that makes one voice or instrument different from another. ---
examples: Her voice has a warm, smoky timbre.
The two guitars differ mostly in timbre.
He can name an instrument by timbre alone.
entries.contrast: Spelled like timber (wood) but said TAM-bur in American English.

entries.meaning: A person or device that measures and records time, especially at a sporting event. ---
examples: The timekeeper stopped the clock with four seconds left.
Two official timekeepers sit at the scorer's table.
My phone is a better timekeeper than that old watch.

entries.meaning: The measuring or recording of time, including hours worked. ---
examples: The company switched to an app for timekeeping.
Accurate timekeeping matters in a race this close.
Sloppy timekeeping cost several workers their overtime.

entries.meaning: Lack of courage or confidence. ---
examples: His timidity in meetings held his career back.
The board was criticized for its timidity.
She got over her timidity by taking a speech class.

entries.meaning: A medicine made by dissolving a substance in alcohol. ---
examples: She takes a tincture of echinacea all winter.
The shelf held a dozen herbal tinctures.
Put ten drops of the tincture under your tongue.

entries.meaning: A place or situation that could burst into violence at any moment. ---
examples: The neighborhood has been a tinderbox since the shooting.
Dry brush turns these canyons into a tinderbox every August.
Both cities are tinderboxes right now.

entries.meaning: Thin metal foil used to wrap or cover food. ---
examples: Cover the pan with tinfoil and bake it for an hour.
He wrapped the leftovers in tinfoil.
Wrap the potatoes in tinfoil before you grill them.
entries.contrast: The package usually says aluminum foil; tinfoil is the everyday spoken word.

entries.meaning: A ringing or buzzing in the ears that has no outside source. ---
examples: Years of loud concerts left him with tinnitus.
Her tinnitus is worst in a quiet room.
There's no cure for tinnitus, but background sound helps.
entries.contrast: Two pronunciations are common in the US: TIN-uh-tuhs and tih-NY-tuhs.

entries.meaning: Shiny strips of foil hung on a Christmas tree for decoration. ---
examples: The tree was covered in silver tinsel.
We were finding tinsel in the carpet until March.
She hates tinsel and puts up plain lights instead.

entries.meaning: A long, angry speech of criticism. ---
examples: He launched into a tirade about the parking rules.
Her tirade went on for twenty minutes.
The coach's tirades are legendary around here.

entries.meaning: An Italian dessert of coffee-soaked cake layered with sweetened cheese. ---
examples: We split a tiramisu after dinner.
Her tiramisu is better than the restaurant's.
There's tiramisu on the dessert menu tonight.

entries.meaning: A person or company of enormous power or importance in some field. ---
examples: He was a titan of the steel industry.
Two titans of tech testified before the committee.
She's a titan in her field but shy in person.

entries.meaning: A small gray songbird with a crest, common at American bird feeders. ---
examples: A tufted titmouse landed on the feeder.
Two titmice chased each other around the yard.
The titmouse takes one seed at a time.
entries.contrast: The plural is titmice, like mice, though the bird has nothing to do with mice.

entries.meaning: A lab method of measuring what a liquid contains by adding another liquid drop by drop. ---
examples: We did an acid-base titration in chemistry lab.
Titration gave us the exact concentration.
The doctor used slow titration to find the right dose.

entries.meaning: A mushroom, especially a poisonous one. ---
examples: Don't touch the red toadstool by the fence.
Toadstools popped up all over the lawn after the rain.
The picture book had a fairy sitting on a toadstool.

entries.meaning: A long flat sled with a curved front, used for sliding down snowy hills. ---
examples: They dragged the toboggan up the hill one more time.
Three kids fit on the toboggan at once.
He steered the toboggan straight into a snowbank.

entries.meaning: The hard covering on the upper tip of a toe. ---
examples: He broke a toenail playing soccer.
She painted her toenails bright red.
An ingrown toenail can get infected fast.

entries.meaning: A loose robe draped around the body, worn by citizens of ancient Rome. ---
examples: The statue shows a senator in a toga.
They wore bedsheet togas to the party.
His toga kept slipping off his shoulder.

entries.meaning: A warm feeling of closeness among people who spend time with each other. ---
examples: The holidays are all about togetherness.
Sunday dinners gave the family a sense of togetherness.
He missed the togetherness of the old office.

entries.meaning: A switch or control with two settings that you flip between. ---
examples: There's a toggle at the top of the settings page.
Flip the toggle to turn on dark mode.
The app has toggles for every kind of notification.

entries.meaning: An item such as soap, shampoo, or toothpaste used for washing and grooming. ---
examples: Pack your toiletries in a clear plastic bag.
The hotel leaves free toiletries in the bathroom.
Shampoo was the one toiletry she forgot.
entries.contrast: Almost always used in the plural: toiletries.

entries.meaning: A small object used in place of money or a ticket, or something that stands as a sign of a feeling. ---
examples: The arcade still runs on tokens.
Please accept this as a token of our thanks.
Each subway token cost a dollar back then.

entries.meaning: A small structure on a road or bridge where drivers pay a toll. ---
examples: We waited ten minutes at the tollbooth.
Most tollbooths on this highway are automated now.
Have your change ready before the tollbooth.

entries.meaning: A light axe used as a tool and a weapon by some Native American peoples. ---
examples: The museum displays a stone tomahawk.
He learned to throw a tomahawk at summer camp.
Two tomahawks hung above the fireplace.

entries.meaning: A small green fruit in a papery husk, used in Mexican sauces. ---
examples: Roast the tomatillos before you blend the salsa.
A tomatillo is firmer and tarter than a tomato.
The market had tomatillos for a dollar a pound.
entries.contrast: The ll is Spanish, so it sounds like a faint y: tah-muh-TEE-oh, never -til-oh.

entries.meaning: A girl who enjoys clothes and activities traditionally seen as boyish. ---
examples: She was a tomboy who lived in jeans and sneakers.
Both sisters were tomboys growing up.
He calls his daughter a tomboy with obvious pride.

entries.meaning: A large, heavy book. ---
examples: He hauled a five-pound tome on Roman law to class.
The library keeps the oldest tomes behind glass.
Her biography is a nine-hundred-page tome.

entries.meaning: The total weight or carrying capacity of cargo or ships, measured in tons. ---
examples: The port's tonnage fell for the third year running.
Tonnage through the canal is up sharply.
They charge by tonnage, not by the truckload.
entries.contrast: The first vowel is the u of ton: TUHN-ij, not TAHN-ij.

entries.meaning: The highest part or upper surface of something. ---
examples: There's dust on the top of the fridge.
We hiked to the top in two hours.
She wore a black top with jeans.

entries.meaning: A hard clear mineral, often golden or blue, cut and used as a gemstone. ---
examples: Her ring holds a pale blue topaz.
Topaz is the birthstone for November.
The case held two topazes and an emerald.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: The shape and surface features of the land in an area. ---
examples: The topography here makes farming difficult.
Rough topography slowed the search party down.
He studied the topography on the map before the hike.

entries.meaning: Forward spin put on a ball so that it dips in the air and kicks forward off the bounce. ---
examples: She hits her forehand with heavy topspin.
Topspin is what keeps the ball inside the baseline.
Put a little topspin on the serve.

entries.meaning: A state of being inactive and mentally dull, or a deep sleep-like state in animals. ---
examples: The afternoon heat put the whole town into a torpor.
Hummingbirds enter torpor on cold nights.
It took two cups of coffee to shake off the torpor.

entries.meaning: A fast violent stream of water, or a heavy rush of anything. ---
examples: Rain came down in torrents all night.
The creek turned into a torrent after the storm.
She got a torrent of angry email about the column.

entries.meaning: The twisting of an object caused by a force applied at one end. ---
examples: The axle failed under torsion.
Torsion bars replaced the springs on that model.
The vet operated for torsion of the stomach.

entries.meaning: A wrongful act, other than breaking a contract, that a person can be sued over. ---
examples: The suit was filed as a tort claim.
Tort reform has been on the ballot twice.
First-year law students spend a whole semester on torts.
entries.contrast: Tort (a legal wrong) sounds exactly like torte (a rich cake).

entries.meaning: A rich dense cake made with ground nuts or very little flour. ---
examples: She brought a chocolate torte to the potluck.
The bakery makes three kinds of tortes.
One slice of that torte is plenty for two people.
entries.contrast: Said the same as tort, the legal term.

entries.meaning: Small ring-shaped pasta stuffed with cheese or meat. ---
examples: We had cheese tortellini in broth.
The tortellini only takes four minutes to cook.
He makes tortellini from scratch every Christmas.

entries.meaning: The deliberate causing of severe pain, or something extremely unpleasant to sit through. ---
examples: The report documented the use of torture.
That three-hour meeting was pure torture.
He confessed under torture and later took it back.

entries.meaning: A light throw, or the flipping of a coin to settle something. ---
examples: The game starts with a coin toss.
One quick toss and the keys were in my hand.
They settled the argument with a toss.

entries.meaning: A flat fried tortilla served with beans, meat, and other toppings piled on top. ---
examples: I ordered two chicken tostadas.
The tostada fell apart when I picked it up.
She layers her tostadas with beans and avocado.

entries.meaning: The whole of something taken together, or the period when a solar eclipse is complete. ---
examples: Judge the plan in its totality, not piece by piece.
Totality lasted almost four minutes in Dallas.
The totality of the evidence points one way.

entries.meaning: An animal or object treated as the emblem of a family, clan, or group. ---
examples: The bear was the clan's totem.
Carved totems line the path to the museum.
That old truck became a kind of family totem.

entries.meaning: The sense that lets you feel things through your skin, or physical contact itself. ---
examples: She could tell the fabric by touch alone.
The cat flinched at his touch.
Let's stay in touch after graduation.

entries.meaning: A unit of local government smaller than a county in some US states. ---
examples: The township plows our road after every storm.
Three townships share one fire department.
He ran for township supervisor and lost by nine votes.

entries.meaning: How poisonous something is, or how harmful a hostile atmosphere is. ---
examples: Tests showed high toxicity in the soil.
The drug's toxicity limits how much you can take.
She quit because of the toxicity in that office.

entries.meaning: A small remaining sign that something was there. ---
examples: There was no trace of the missing hikers.
The lab found traces of lead in the water.
A trace of a smile crossed his face.

entries.meaning: The work of following something back to its source or along its path. ---
examples: Contact tracing helped slow the outbreak.
Tracing the money took investigators two years.
The site makes tracing your family line pretty easy.

entries.meaning: A device or program that follows the position or progress of something, or a person skilled at following trails. ---
examples: She wears a fitness tracker on her wrist.
The package has a GPS tracker taped inside.
The park hired an experienced tracker to help search.

entries.meaning: A situation where you accept less of one good thing to get more of another. ---
examples: The lighter frame is a tradeoff for strength.
Every schedule involves tradeoffs.
There's a real tradeoff between speed and accuracy.
entries.contrast: Often written with a hyphen, trade-off; both spellings are common in the US.

entries.meaning: The buying and selling of goods, stocks, or currency. ---
examples: Trading on the exchange stopped for an hour after the crash.
He made a small fortune in online trading.
Trading was light the day before the holiday.

entries.meaning: Someone who is the first to do something and opens the way for others. ---
examples: She was a trailblazer for women in engineering.
The founders are considered trailblazers in solar power.
He called his old coach a real trailblazer.

entries.meaning: Someone who is learning a job while working at it. ---
examples: She started as a trainee and now runs the department.
The bank hires about fifty trainees every summer.
A trainee shadowed me for the whole shift.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable: tray-NEE, not TRAY-nee.

entries.meaning: The curved path an object follows through the air, or the general direction in which something develops. ---
examples: The rocket left its planned trajectory within seconds.
Her career has been on an upward trajectory since 2019.
The two countries are on very different economic trajectories.

entries.meaning: A homeless person who travels from place to place. ---
examples: An old tramp was sleeping under the bridge.
The novel follows two tramps riding freight trains.
He looked like a tramp after three days of camping.

entries.meaning: One portion of a larger sum of money, released or sold separately. ---
examples: The first tranche of aid arrives next month.
Investors bought the safer tranches of the loan.
The grant is paid out in three tranches.
entries.contrast: Borrowed from French: the -che is said like sh, TRAHNSH.

entries.meaning: A state of calm and quiet. ---
examples: We drove out to the lake for a weekend of tranquility.
Nothing disturbs the tranquility of that valley.
She found real tranquility in the monastery garden.
entries.contrast: Americans usually write tranquility with one l; the British spell it tranquillity.

entries.meaning: A drug given to calm a person or animal down. ---
examples: The vet used a tranquilizer to move the injured bear.
He has been on mild tranquilizers since the accident.
The dart gun fires a tranquilizer.
entries.contrast: American English spells it tranquilizer; British English writes tranquilliser.

entries.meaning: The process of changing from one state or system to another. ---
examples: The transition to the new software took three months.
Both transitions of power went smoothly.
She is in transition between jobs right now.

entries.meaning: A device that sends out radio or television signals. ---
examples: Lightning knocked out the station's transmitter.
The researchers fitted the wolves with radio transmitters.
A tiny transmitter in the collar tracks the dog.

entries.meaning: A device that receives a signal and automatically sends one back, used on aircraft and toll roads. ---
examples: The plane's transponder stopped sending data over the ocean.
Stick the toll transponder on your windshield.
Both transponders failed the preflight check.

entries.meaning: The moving of people or goods from one place to another. ---
examples: The company handles the transport of frozen food.
Air transport is faster but far more expensive.
Transport of the equipment took two full days.
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed TRANS-port, the verb trans-PORT. For the public system Americans normally say transportation.

entries.meaning: Behavior that betrays someone who trusted you. ---
examples: He never forgave his brother's treachery.
The play is full of treachery and revenge.
She saw the leak to the press as pure treachery.

entries.meaning: An exercise machine with a moving belt that you walk or run on. ---
examples: I do thirty minutes on the treadmill every morning.
All the treadmills at the gym were taken.
He hates running outside, so he bought a treadmill.
entries.contrast: The first syllable is TRED, rhyming with bed, even though it is spelled like tread.

entries.meaning: Gold, jewels, and other riches, or a single object of great value. ---
examples: Divers found buried treasure in the wreck.
The museum's greatest treasures are on the second floor.
That old map is a real treasure.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The person who looks after the money of a club, company, or organization. ---
examples: She was elected treasurer of the parent association.
Both treasurers signed the annual report.
Ask the treasurer how much is left in the fund.

entries.meaning: A long, serious piece of writing on one subject. ---
examples: He wrote a treatise on constitutional law.
The library keeps medieval treatises on medicine.
Her essay reads more like a treatise than a blog post.
entries.contrast: Spelled -tise but said with an s sound: TREE-tis.

entries.meaning: A feeling of fear or worry about something that is about to happen. ---
examples: She opened the letter with some trepidation.
There was a lot of trepidation before the first day of school.
He approached the interview with obvious trepidation.

entries.meaning: The offense of going onto someone's land or property without permission. ---
examples: He was arrested for trespass on railroad property.
The sign warns that trespass will be prosecuted.
The case turned on whether walking the trail counted as trespass.
entries.contrast: The sign posted everywhere in the United States reads "No Trespassing", with the -ing form.

entries.meaning: Strong loyalty to your own group, often combined with hostility toward outsiders. ---
examples: Commentators blame tribalism for the gridlock in Congress.
Sports tribalism is mostly harmless.
The article traces the rise of political tribalism.

entries.meaning: The large muscle at the back of the upper arm. ---
examples: These push-ups work the triceps.
He tore his triceps lifting weights.
Her triceps are more developed than her biceps.
entries.contrast: The singular already ends in -s, and the plural is also triceps.

entries.meaning: A large plant-eating dinosaur with three horns on its head. ---
examples: The museum's triceratops skull is enormous.
My son can tell a triceratops from a stegosaurus.
Two triceratops skeletons came out of the same quarry.
entries.contrast: The plural is normally the same as the singular: two triceratops.

entries.meaning: A clever act done to entertain people or to deceive them. ---
examples: The dog knows three tricks.
That's an old trick salesmen use.
There's a trick to opening this window.

entries.meaning: The use of dishonest methods to cheat or fool people. ---
examples: The contract was signed through outright trickery.
He won the game by skill, not trickery.
There was no magic in it, just trickery.

entries.meaning: A spear with three points. ---
examples: The statue shows the sea god holding a trident.
Gladiators fought with nets and tridents.
The team's logo is a silver trident.

entries.meaning: The number one million million, written 1,000,000,000,000. ---
examples: The national debt passed thirty trillion dollars.
Trillions of cells make up the human body.
The plan would cost about a trillion over ten years.

entries.meaning: A set of three books or films that tell one connected story. ---
examples: I read the whole trilogy over the summer.
The studio is planning a trilogy.
Both trilogies were filmed back to back.

entries.meaning: A three-legged stand that holds a camera or telescope steady. ---
examples: Set the camera on a tripod for night shots.
The photographers lined up their tripods along the fence.
I forgot the tripod, so every picture is blurry.

entries.meaning: A great victory or success. ---
examples: The election was a personal triumph for the mayor.
The film was a triumph with critics.
She lists her small daily triumphs in a notebook.

entries.meaning: A musician who plays the trombone. ---
examples: The band needs a second trombonist.
He is the best trombonist in the state.
Two trombonists stood up for the solo.

entries.meaning: A state police officer, or a soldier in a cavalry or armored unit. ---
examples: A state trooper pulled us over near the border.
Two troopers blocked off the highway.
Her father was a trooper for twenty years.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like trouper, a person who keeps going cheerfully: "she's a real trouper".

entries.meaning: A familiar idea, image, or plot device that keeps turning up in stories. ---
examples: The lonely detective is a well-worn trope.
The show plays with classic horror tropes.
That's a tired trope about small towns.

entries.meaning: Difficulty or worry, or a particular problem that causes it. ---
examples: He's in serious trouble at work.
The car gave us no trouble on the trip.
She listened patiently to all my troubles.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: Someone who deliberately causes problems for other people. ---
examples: The teacher moved the two troublemakers apart.
He got a reputation as a troublemaker in high school.
Management labeled her a troublemaker after the walkout.

entries.meaning: Staying away from school without permission. ---
examples: The district is trying to cut truancy in half.
Truancy rose sharply after the pandemic.
He was sent to court for chronic truancy.

entries.meaning: An expensive underground fungus used in cooking, or a soft round chocolate candy. ---
examples: The pasta was shaved with black truffle.
She gave me a box of chocolate truffles.
Dogs are trained to sniff out truffles.

entries.meaning: A musician who plays the trumpet. ---
examples: The trumpeter played the national anthem.
Miles Davis was the trumpeter everyone imitated.
Three trumpeters stood at the back of the stage.

entries.meaning: A person appointed to manage money or property for someone else, or a member of a governing board. ---
examples: The board of trustees meets in April.
Her uncle is the trustee of the family fund.
Two trustees voted against the tuition increase.
entries.contrast: Stressed on the last syllable, trus-TEE — unlike trusty, said TRUS-tee.

entries.meaning: A small bunch of hair, grass, or feathers growing or held together. ---
examples: A tuft of white hair stuck up on the back of his head.
Tufts of grass grew between the paving stones.
The owl has dark tufts above its eyes.

entries.meaning: A short, strong pull. ---
examples: She felt a tug on the fishing line.
Give the rope a couple of tugs when you're ready.
He felt a tug of guilt as he drove away.

entries.meaning: A dry desert plant that breaks off at the root and rolls along the ground in the wind. ---
examples: A tumbleweed blew across the empty highway.
Tumbleweeds piled up against the fence overnight.
The town was so quiet you half expected a tumbleweed.

entries.meaning: A very hard gray metal with an extremely high melting point. ---
examples: Old light bulbs used a tungsten filament.
The drill bits are tipped with tungsten.
His wedding ring is made of tungsten.

entries.meaning: A loose garment reaching from the shoulders to the hips or knees, usually without a collar. ---
examples: She wore a linen tunic over leggings.
The actors wore Roman tunics.
His uniform tunic had brass buttons.

entries.meaning: The chance to do something in an agreed order, or a change of direction. ---
examples: It's your turn to drive.

The kids took turns on the swing.

entries.meaning: A nasal quality in someone's accent, or the sharp sound of a plucked string. ---

His voice lost its country twang after years in Boston.

entries.meaning: A sudden short pain, or a brief uncomfortable feeling. ---
examples: I felt a twinge in my back when I stood up.
He had a twinge of guilt about leaving early.
The old injury still gives her twinges in cold weather.

entries.meaning: A small flickering light, or a lively look in someone's eyes. ---
examples: He told the story with a twinkle in his eye.

There was a mischievous twinkle in her expression.

entries.meaning: A small sudden movement of a muscle that you cannot control. ---
examples: He has a nervous twitch under his left eye.
The dog's ear gave a twitch.
Tiny twitches in his hands gave away how nervous he was.

entries.meaning: A serious infectious disease caught from contaminated food or water. ---
examples: Travelers to the region are vaccinated against typhoid.
The outbreak of typhoid was traced to a single well.
She spent a month in the hospital with typhoid.
entries.contrast: Typhoid and typhus are two different diseases, spread in completely different ways.

entries.meaning: A serious infectious disease spread by lice and fleas, causing fever and a rash. ---
examples: Typhus swept through the camps that winter.
He died of typhus in 1943.
Crowded, dirty conditions helped typhus spread.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse typhus with typhoid — despite the similar names they are separate diseases.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is typing documents. ---
examples: She worked as a typist in a law office.
The agency still employs two typists.
He's a fast typist but a terrible speller.

entries.meaning: A ruler or boss who uses power cruelly and unfairly. ---
examples: The country was run by a tyrant for thirty years.
History books are full of tyrants.
Our old manager was a petty tyrant.

entries.meaning: The quality of being unpleasant to look at, or of being nasty and hostile. ---
examples: He photographs the ugliness of the industrial coast.
There was real ugliness in the comments online.
The ugliness of the argument shocked everyone.

entries.meaning: Light just beyond the violet end of the spectrum, invisible to the eye and able to burn skin. ---
examples: Sunscreen blocks most ultraviolet from reaching the skin.
The lamp gives off ultraviolet to kill bacteria.
Snow reflects a surprising amount of ultraviolet.

entries.meaning: A piece of underwear worn on the lower body. ---
examples: Pack extra socks and underpants.
He walked to the kitchen in his underpants.
The store sells three pairs of underpants for ten dollars.
entries.contrast: Plural only, like pants — one garment is "a pair of underpants".

entries.meaning: A task or project, especially a large and difficult one. ---
examples: Rebuilding the bridge was a huge undertaking.
The move turned into a bigger undertaking than we expected.
Both undertakings ran well over budget.
entries.contrast: Stressed un-dur-TAY-king in this sense; stressed UN-dur-tay-king it means the funeral business.

entries.meaning: A quality or feeling that is present but not stated openly, or a very quiet voice. ---
examples: The speech had an angry undertone.
The comedy has surprisingly dark undertones.
They argued in undertones so the baby wouldn't wake up.

entries.meaning: The world of organized crime, or the world of the dead in ancient myths. ---
examples: He spent years reporting on the city's underworld.
In the myth she travels to the underworld to find her husband.
The killing looked like underworld score-settling.

entries.meaning: The cause of someone's failure or ruin. ---
examples: His temper was his undoing.
Overconfidence proved to be the team's undoing.
Greed was the undoing of the whole company.

entries.meaning: The quality of treating people in a way that is not just or equal. ---
examples: Students complained about the unfairness of the grading.
She could not get over the unfairness of it.
The article documents the unfairness of the old system.

entries.meaning: A feeling of sadness or dissatisfaction. ---
examples: There was obvious unhappiness among the staff.
He hid his unhappiness well.
The survey measured unhappiness with the new schedule.

entries.meaning: An imaginary white horse with a single horn on its forehead. ---
examples: Her backpack is covered in unicorns.
The tapestry shows a unicorn in a walled garden.
In tech, a startup worth a billion dollars is called a unicorn.

entries.meaning: The process of workers forming or joining a labor union. ---
examples: Unionization at the warehouse took two years.
The company fought unionization every step of the way.
Unionization rates have fallen since the 1970s.
entries.contrast: American English spells it unionization; British English writes unionisation.

entries.meaning: The state of doing or saying something at exactly the same time as others. ---
examples: The whole class answered in unison.
The dancers moved in perfect unison.
The choir sang the first verse in unison.

entries.meaning: A big, sudden, and usually unsettling change. ---
examples: The merger caused months of upheaval at the office.
The country went through political upheaval after the election.
Her childhood was a series of upheavals.

entries.meaning: A small increase in something. ---
examples: Hospitals reported an uptick in flu cases.
There was a modest uptick in sales last quarter.
Small upticks in traffic don't mean much.

entries.meaning: An improvement, especially in business or the economy. ---
examples: Dealers are hoping for an upturn in the spring.
The upturn came later than economists predicted.
Past upturns have always followed a rate cut.

entries.meaning: The process by which more and more people come to live in cities. ---
examples: Rapid urbanization has strained the water supply.
Urbanization changed the country in a single generation.
The map shows urbanization spreading along the coast.
entries.contrast: American English spells it urbanization; British English writes urbanisation.

entries.meaning: The act of using something, or a purpose that something can serve. ---
examples: The use of cell phones is banned during the exam.
This tool has a hundred uses around the house.
What's the use of arguing about it now?
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
entries.contrast: The noun ends in an s sound, YOOS; the verb use ends in a z sound, YOOZ.

entries.meaning: Someone who seizes power or a position by force and without the right to it. ---
examples: The general was branded a usurper by the exiled king.
History books treat him as a usurper, not a legitimate ruler.
The play is about two usurpers fighting over a stolen throne.

entries.meaning: The practice of lending money at an unfairly high rate of interest. ---
examples: State law caps interest rates to prevent usury.
Payday lenders have been accused of usury.
Usury was condemned by the medieval church.

entries.meaning: The extent to which something available is actually put to use. ---
examples: The hospital tracks bed utilization every night.
Better utilization of the new software would save hours a week.
Factory utilization fell to sixty percent.
entries.contrast: English utilization means putting something to use; Russian «утилизация» means disposal or recycling — a false friend.

entries.meaning: An imagined place where everything is perfect. ---
examples: The novel describes a technological utopia with no work and no illness.
Their commune was supposed to be a utopia.
Every generation dreams up its own utopias.

entries.meaning: Something a person says, treated as a single piece of speech. ---
examples: Her first utterance of the morning was a complaint about the coffee.
Linguists record thousands of utterances from ordinary conversation.
The child's early utterances were only one word long.

entries.meaning: Someone who is away from home on vacation. ---
examples: Summer vacationers fill every motel on the coast.
A vacationer from Ohio found the wallet on the beach.
The island lives on money from vacationers.
entries.contrast: Americans say vacationer; the British equivalent is holidaymaker.

entries.meaning: A person who moves from place to place with no home or steady job. ---
examples: He spent his twenties as a cheerful vagabond, working just enough to eat.
The old song is about a vagabond riding freight trains.
The town had little patience for vagabonds.

entries.meaning: An unpredictable change or turn in something. ---
examples: Farmers here live with the vagaries of the weather.
The vagaries of the stock market wiped out his gains.
One vagary of the tax code lets them deduct the whole cost.
entries.contrast: It almost always appears in the plural, in the phrase the vagaries of something.

entries.meaning: The passage in a woman's body leading from the uterus to the outside. ---
examples: The doctor explained how the vagina changes after childbirth.
Health class covered the vagina and the rest of the reproductive system.
The medication is inserted into the vagina.

entries.meaning: The condition of living on the streets with no home or work, often treated as an offense. ---
examples: He was arrested for vagrancy in 1962.
The city repealed its old vagrancy laws.
Vagrancy rose sharply after the factories closed.

entries.meaning: A person with no home or regular work who wanders from place to place. ---
examples: A vagrant was sleeping in the doorway.
Police moved the vagrants out of the park.
He looked like a vagrant after three weeks on the road.

entries.meaning: The quality of not being clear or exact. ---
examples: The vagueness of the contract worried our lawyer.
Voters complained about the vagueness of his promises.
There is a certain vagueness in her answers.
entries.contrast: The u is silent — vague rhymes with plague: VAYG.

entries.meaning: The number of chemical bonds an atom can form with other atoms. ---
examples: Carbon has a valence of four.
The teacher drew the valence electrons around each atom.
Different valences explain why the two metals react so differently.

entries.meaning: Proof or recognition that something is correct, worthwhile, or officially accepted. ---
examples: The award felt like validation after years of rejection.
The form requires validation by a supervisor.
She looks for validation from everyone around her.

entries.meaning: The quality of being sound and well founded, or of being legally in force. ---
examples: No one questions the validity of the results.
Check the validity of your passport before you book.
The judge doubted the validity of that argument.

entries.meaning: A small possession that is worth a lot of money. ---
examples: Leave your valuables in the hotel safe.
The thieves took every valuable in the house.
She keeps her valuables in a locked drawer.
entries.contrast: As a noun it is nearly always plural — valuables; the singular is usually the adjective.

entries.meaning: A creature in stories that rises at night and drinks people's blood. ---
examples: The kids dressed up as vampires for Halloween.
The movie is about a vampire living quietly in Detroit.
In the legend a vampire cannot cross running water.

entries.meaning: A person who deliberately damages property belonging to others. ---
examples: Vandals smashed every window in the dugout.
The school is hunting for the vandal who spray-painted the doors.
Police charged two vandals with destruction of property.

entries.meaning: The group leading the way in a movement or a new development. ---
examples: The lab is in the vanguard of cancer research.
These painters were the vanguard of a whole new style.
Her company stayed in the vanguard for a decade.

entries.meaning: A position that gives a good view or a good perspective on something. ---
examples: From that vantage you can see the whole valley.
The ridge gave the scouts an excellent vantage.
He wrote the history from the vantage of fifty years later.
entries.contrast: You will hear it most often in the phrase vantage point.

entries.meaning: A device that turns liquid into vapor, used for medicine or for adding moisture to the air. ---
examples: We run a vaporizer in the baby's room when she has a cold.
The pharmacy sells small vaporizers for about twenty dollars.
He filled the vaporizer with distilled water.

entries.meaning: The extent to which something changes or differs from case to case. ---
examples: There is huge variability in how patients respond.
Rainfall variability makes farming risky here.
The study measured variability between the two groups.

entries.meaning: The amount by which two things differ or fail to agree. ---
examples: His account is at variance with the video.
There was little variance between the two estimates.
The report explains the variance in monthly costs.

entries.meaning: A change in something, or a slightly different form of it. ---
examples: This recipe is a variation on my grandmother's.
There are regional variations in how the word is pronounced.
Small variations in temperature ruin the whole batch.

entries.meaning: The top team representing a school or college in a sport. ---
examples: He made varsity as a sophomore.
The varsity plays at seven; junior varsity plays at four.
She was captain of the varsity soccer team.
entries.contrast: In the U.S. varsity is the school's top team; in Britain it is an old slang word for a university.

entries.meaning: In the Middle Ages, a man who held land from a lord in return for loyalty and service. ---
examples: Each vassal owed the king forty days of military service.
The duke's vassals met at the castle every spring.
The treaty reduced the smaller country to a vassal of its neighbor.

entries.meaning: A quantity that has both size and direction, or an animal that carries a disease from one host to another. ---
examples: Draw the force as a vector pointing to the right.

The graphics are stored as vectors, so they never look blurry.

entries.meaning: The plants growing in a particular area, taken together. ---

There is almost no vegetation above the tree line.

entries.meaning: A long, bitter campaign of revenge against a person or family. ---
examples: He has a personal vendetta against his old boss.

entries.meaning: A thin layer of fine material covering something cheaper, or an outward appearance that hides the truth. ---

entries.meaning: Punishment inflicted in return for a wrong. ---

entries.meaning: A machine that breathes for a patient who cannot breathe well enough alone. ---

entries.meaning: One of the two lower chambers of the heart, or a hollow space inside the brain. ---

entries.meaning: The quality of being true, or of telling the truth. ---

entries.meaning: Wording, especially wording that is longer or fancier than it needs to be. ---

Marketing changed the verbiage on the label.

entries.meaning: The point at which something is about to happen. ---

They stood at the verge of a major discovery.

entries.meaning: The process of checking that something is true or accurate. ---

entries.meaning: Very thin pasta made in long strands. ---
examples: The soup has vermicelli in it.

The ceiling was painted with symbols of the zodiac.
Her column explains the zodiac sign by sign.

entries.meaning: In horror stories, a dead body brought back to life and able to walk. ---
examples: The show is about survivors of a zombie outbreak.
Zombies shuffled toward the fence.
After two nights without sleep I felt like a zombie.

entries.meaning: An area set apart by a particular purpose, rule, or quality. ---
examples: Parking is not allowed in the loading zone.
The city divided the area into three residential zones.
Slow down — you're in a school zone.

entries.meaning: Tiny animals that drift in the sea and are eaten by fish and whales. ---
examples: Whales filter zooplankton out of the water.
Warmer water has reduced the zooplankton in the bay.
The samples were full of zooplankton.

entries.meaning: The single cell formed when an egg and a sperm join.
examples: The zygote begins to divide within hours.
Every human being starts as a single zygote.
The lab studied zygotes under a microscope.
